extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of humorous/parodic poetry (magazine audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or analysing humorous parodies and mock-imitations of established poetic styles (vers de société, blank verse, Celtic symbolism, Whitmanian catalogues, ballades, song-parodies, regional dialect verse) as found in a humour magazine anthology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realist style markers (as satirised)
rubrics_metrics.description: Realist verse is described as 'trenchant, and terse, and cold', 'stooping to dig in dust-heaps', 'sharing the common mold', 'driving a quill quotidian', 'mending a muddy plot', 'sitting in mud-walled prisons', 'steeping their souls in rot' — i.e., an emphasis on mundane, scientific detail and bleak, workmanlike prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To imitate (or satirise) Realism: use terse, blunt diction; foreground ordinary, dirty or workaday imagery; evince a workshop/scientific frame of mind that 'cuts up' romantic embellishment. The piece exemplifies the anti-romantic, matter-of-fact aesthetic and the notion of authors as 'slaves of science'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celtic-style tropes (satirical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Celtic poems are mocked as recurrently using images like the 'wind-swept star', 'Snow-White Bird', 'tricksy Elves', 'Bad Banshee', 'Yellow Wolf-Hound', 'voice of the limitless lake', frequent capitalised Abstract Nouns and 'symbolic' notation; metre irregularities are permitted 'because it's Celtic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To mimic Celtic-renaissance verse: include recurring mystical images (wind-swept star appears repeatedly), archaic/folkloric nouns, symbolic capitalisation, elfin or banshee figures, and an intentionally nebulous 'intimate vision'. Critics are said to reward these repeated stock motifs, so exaggerate them for parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank-verse grandiloquence / meta-defensive posture
rubrics_metrics.description: A mock-blank-verse piece prefaces itself: 'please clearly understand this is blank verse... If it reads strangely, and the accent falls / In unexpected places, do not dare / To criticise. Remember once for all, / That I and Milton judge questions like that.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodying blank verse can involve (a) declaring the form and pre-empting criticism, (b) intentionally displacing expected stresses and enjambments, and (c) adopting a self-important, Miltonic tone coupled with comic triviality (e.g., turning nursery-rhyme content into solemn blank verse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vers de société / chant-royal features
rubrics_metrics.description: Social light-verse and formal stanzas (chant royal) use a repeated refrain ('Behold the deeds that are done of Mrs. Jones!'), episodic stanzas enumerating annoyances, and a final envoy summarising or addressing the group ('Boarders! the worst I have not told to ye').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To write (or lampoon) vers de société: employ a regular stanzaic form, a running refrain that returns exactly each stanza, witty complaints or social anecdotes in each stanza, and a short envoy that addresses the intended audience; keep tone urbane and arch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloquial/dialect-comic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialected comic verse (e.g., 'O CRIKEY Bill!') foregrounds conversational slang, phonetic spellings ('ses', 'blooming peckish'), comic understatement, and the juxtaposition of low-register speech with mock-epic sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create comic dialect verse: render speech phonetically, use idiomatic exclamations and rapid conversational rhythm, and exploit the clash between colloquial phrasing and elevated comic situations for humour. Beware of stereotypes — here it's used for satirical colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballade conventions and self-referential mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Ballade form features repeated rhetorical questions, a refrain ('And who was the Man in the Iron Mask?') and an envoy; the poem plays with the notion that ballades 'always contrive to get lost' and revels in irrelevance and rhetorical accumulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To write or parody a ballade: include the fixed refrain, ask a string of increasingly tangential questions or images, and finish with a short envoy that collapses the poem into a mordant witticism; use the form to lampoon obsessive or forgetful poetic voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song/chorus-parody techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies of popular songs replicate refrains and chorus structure, use repeated vocables and stretched syllables ('Beau—ootiful Soo—oop!'), and subvert the original sentiment by flipping imagery (e.g., 'snow... pure for a minute, then dirty as mud').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To parody a song: copy its chorus/refrain pattern and sound devices (repetition, elongation), then invert or undercut the original sentiment in the verses for comic effect; preserve sing-song cadence to make the parody recognisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swinburne/lyric decadence signals (imitative list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swinburne-like variation uses sea-foam, winds, lush alliteration, fevered rhetorical parenthesis and musical excess ('As sea-foam blown of the winds... The salt of us stings and is sore...'); long, ornate lines and eroticised diction are characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To imitate Swinburne: employ rollicking alliteration, long periodic sentences, sensual imagery drawn from sea/wind, and musical but excessive phrasing; exaggerate the metre and ornament for parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bret Harte / Western-colour mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Western-coloured parody features colloquial frontier dialect, local-colour details (Remington, rancho, griddle-cake), persona-driven anecdote, and rough-hewn humour grounded in everyday survival and boasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To mimic Bret Harte: use region-specific vocabulary and speech rhythms, tell an anecdotal narrative with ironic pride or pathos, and foreground rustic characters and objects as cultural markers; amplify mis-spellings and phonetic contractions for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horatian/roundeau/pastoral translation-imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dobson/Horace pastiches present concise, classical forms (rondeau) with controlled rhyme, restrained diction, and emphasis on home comforts and modest joys ('At home alone... With home-made wine and books that please').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To imitate classical/rondeau style: adopt tight stanzaic controls, balanced periodic phrasing, classical allusions rendered in domestic terms, and a calm, polished tone; in parody, contrast the polished form with trivial subject matter for humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whitmanian free-verse catalogue and democratic celebration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman parodies feature long free-verse lines, direct address to specific readers ('You over there, young man with the guide-book'), catalogues of scenes and types, exuberant colloquial interjections ('Whoop!!!'), and celebration of common life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke Whitman: use long anaphoric lines, enumerate ordinary people/items in extended catalogues, speak directly to the reader, and combine high enthusiasm with plain speech; exaggerate expansiveness and rhetorical self-regard to comic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody-as-method: identify, isolate, exaggerate stock tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Across the pieces the implied method for successful parody is to identify a style's recurring motifs, formal devices, diction and cadence (meter, refrains, stock images), then exaggerate or misapply them to trivial or incongruous subject matter (nursery rhyme, kitchen-soup, boarding-house grievance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: (1) pick target poet/style, (2) list its typical words, images and structures, (3) reproduce those surface features faithfully, (4) substitute mundane or absurd content, and (5) tilt diction/metric choices slightly off-kilter (displaced accents, over-long lines) to highlight the comic contrast. The anthology shows many worked examples.
